blocks.text: OpenAI 最近公布了自 GPT-3.5 以来训练过的 13 个模型的基础模型对数困惑度，测量数据来自其自有代码库中一个固定的留出数据集。数据显示，预训练损失的下降出现了非常惊人的加速：自 2026 年初以来，其下降速度约为 2022 年至 2025 年期间的七倍。

公布
了自 GPT-3.5 以来训练过的 13 个模型的基础模型对数困惑度，测量数据来自其自有代码库中一个固定的留出数据集。数据显示，预训练损失的下降出现了非常惊人的加速：自 2026 年初以来，其下降速度约为 2022 年至 2025 年期间的七倍。

blocks.alt: Scatter plot of log-perplexity on OpenAI's held-out dataset against model release date, from GPT-3.5 (2022) to 2026 models, with a two-segment linear fit. From 2022 to early 2026 log-perplexity falls slowly (about 0.022 per year); after a breakpoint in February 2026 it falls about 0.156 per year, 7.1 times steeper. OpenAI's internal model is shown as a hollow square and is not used in the fit.

blocks.text: 如果保持当前速度，OpenAI 将在大约六个半月内走完 GPT-3.5 到 GPT-4.1 之间耗时三年的对数困惑度降幅。这一加速之所以更令人惊讶，是因为损失上的进展本应随时间越来越难：文本永远无法被完美预测，因此损失不可能低于某个下限，而随着模型逼近该下限，收益通常也会变小。按照标准缩放定律，计算量每增加十倍，带来的损失降幅都比上一次更小，所以按直觉预期，损失上的进展本应随时间放缓（见下图）。1

blocks.alt: Illustrative schematic with fake data. Log-perplexity against time, with dotted lines for a few possible loss floors above zero and a dashed curve for each showing the default expectation: progress slows as the loss approaches its floor. The observed 2026 pattern instead shows progress speeding up, with the most recent points falling below all of the dashed curves. A hard floor at zero is marked.

blocks.text: METR 的员工内部仍在积极讨论如何解读预训练进展的这一剧烈加速，以及如何将其与 OpenAI 模型基准分数缺乏相应加速这一现象相协调，例如 Epoch 的 ECI 所反映的情况。

blocks.text: 具体来说，这一新信息应在多大程度上改变我们对未来 AI 能力的预测，仍有争议。以下几点考量很重要：

inlines.text: 具体来说，这一新信息应在多大程度上改变我们对未来 AI 能力的预测，仍有争议。以下几点考量很重要：
公布的数据有可能夸大了预训练的真实进展，例如通过各类过拟合。更多数据在这方面会有很大帮助。
基准分数有可能才是衡量现实世界能力的最佳指标，而预训练困惑度只作为输入信息有意义。这意味着，显示预训练进展加速的新数据不会实质性改变我们对未来能力的预测。
不过，如果 AI 确实促成了预训练的加速，这就能让我们一窥 AI 未来可能在模型训练全流程各环节中作出的贡献。
预训练困惑度有可能反映的是比评估模型常用的典型基准更为根本的模型能力度量。许多 AI 研究者就是这样看待预训练困惑度的，他们预计 OpenAI 在预训练上的快速加速之后，会迎来以现实世界影响来衡量的能力加速。

blocks.text: 对于这一信息应在多大程度上修正我们对未来能力发展路径的预测，仍存在重大分歧，METR 内部对此没有共识。一些解读意味着，OpenAI 关于预训练加速的数据应让我们预期，未来六个月现实世界 AI 能力将出现广泛的加速。

inlines.text: 对于这一信息应在多大程度上修正我们对未来能力发展路径的预测，仍存在重大分歧，METR 内部对此没有共识。一些解读意味着，OpenAI 关于预训练加速的数据应让我们预期，未来六个月现实世界 AI 能力将出现广泛的加速。

blocks.text: 据我们所知，此前没有任何前沿模型开发者公开过：在固定的留出数据集上，其历代前沿模型的预训练损失在多年间是如何变化的。这类信息通常被视为高度商业敏感。不过我们认为，公开预训练损失的信息很有价值，有助于让公众了解 AI 研发加速的前景。我们鼓励所有 AI 开发者都这样做——微软已经用 OpenAI 的数据集做了同样的事——并分享更多背景信息，让外部研究者能更好地理解加速的程度、驱动因素，以及我们是否应当预期这种加速会持续和/或叠加。5

inlines.text: 据我们所知，此前没有任何前沿模型开发者公开过：在固定的留出数据集上，其历代前沿模型的预训练损失在多年间是如何变化的。这类信息通常被视为高度商业敏感。不过我们认为，公开预训练损失的信息很有价值，有助于让公众了解 AI 研发加速的前景。我们鼓励所有 AI 开发者都这样做——微软已经用 OpenAI 的数据集
做了
同样的事——并分享更多背景信息，让外部研究者能更好地理解加速的程度、驱动因素，以及我们是否应当预期这种加速会持续和/或叠加。

blocks.text: 以下信息会特别有帮助：

inlines.text: 以下信息会特别有帮助：
在其他留出数据集上的对数困惑度。
在单一语料上测得的损失，未必能反映在其他类型文本上的进展。例如，OpenAI 的图表报告的是取自其内部代码库的语料上的损失。较新的训练配方或数据，可能对这类文本（如编程）的帮助大于其他文本；也可能代码库的一小部分已经泄漏进了训练数据。在其他差异很大的留出数据集（例如书籍语料）上测对数困惑度，能说明这一趋势是否稳健。
最终，这些留出语料可以由第三方维护，从而能够比较不同 AI 开发者的预训练损失趋势。
每个模型预训练运行结束的大致日期。

按模型的公开发布日期来作图，可能无法反映预训练进展实际发生的时间：对数困惑度是基座模型的属性，而基座模型可能在发布前几个月就已完成。如果预训练运行结束到模型发布之间的滞后期随时间缩短，那么损失的加速幅度会比图表显示的小（反之亦然）。更重要的是，了解滞后期有助于判断 AI 对预训练增益的贡献有多大：无论模型何时发布，如果它的预训练发生在研究者几乎不使用 AI 智能体的时期，我们就不能把它的预训练增益归因于 AI 智能体。
预训练算力、人力支出和实验算力随时间的变化。
预训练损失降低可能归因于多种因素：例如训练算力增加、人力或实验算力支出增加，或 AI 辅助带来的提升增加。其中一些因素意味着我们应当预期这种增长是一次性尖峰，另一些则意味着应当预期它会持续；如果它在很大程度上归因于 AI 的提升，加速就可能叠加。要理解这一点，了解相关时期内这些资源如何增长会很有帮助。
脚注
一种理解方式是：把对数困惑度换算成“有效算力”，即单一固定配方达到某一损失值所需的算力。如果我们假设 OpenAI 的所有模型都遵循同一条缩放定律、不可约损失在 0.3 到 0.6 之间，那么以每年数量级衡量，自 2026 年初以来有效算力的增长速度大约比 2022–2025 年快 8 到 10 倍。但这个假设并不现实，因为较新的配方很可能遵循不同的缩放定律。
比如，有些架构改动会让每个 token 消耗更多算力（例如循环 Transformer），这类改动对困惑度的降低可能大于对下游能力的提升，因为标准模型在训练后通过思维链推理也能达到相近的能力。
OpenAI 文章中的
一条脚注
与这一判断相符：AI 在加速初期作用较小，但目前作用更大。“我们主要将其归因于长期研究和算力投入的成果，自动化只占较小部分。不过，对于最新的模型，我们已经看到 AI 做出了有意义的设计贡献。”同样，METR 近期对 Anthropic 内部 AI 研发加速的
评估
发现，2025 年末的加速可能受到非 AI 因素的影响，但估计“当前（2026 年 10 月）加速的大部分（也许约 80%）应归因于 AI。”
还有一个相关论点可以解释，为什么这些预训练加速的数据应当改变我们对现实世界能力的预测：我们用来衡量能力的量表，比如 ECI、
MCI
和时间跨度，对细微的统计假设很敏感，或者严重依赖少数几个接近饱和的基准测试。
还有很多其他类型的信息也会有帮助，但我们聚焦于几个数字，这些数字我们认为公司已经在收集，分享起来也应该相对简单。
其他留出数据集应当来自 2022 年之前，这样就不会包含任何 AI 生成的文本。理想情况下，它们应覆盖多种文本类型，比如代码、科学写作和散文，以便看出原始留出集上的趋势有多少具体反映了代码方面的进展。

blocks.text: OpenAI recently published the base-model log-perplexity of 13 models it has trained since GPT-3.5, measured on a fixed held-out dataset sourced from its own codebase. It shows a very striking acceleration in pretraining loss: since early 2026, it has been falling about seven times faster than it was from 2022 through 2025.

From 2022 to early 2026 log-perplexity falls slowly (about 0.022 per year); after a breakpoint in February 2026 it falls about 0.156 per year, 7.1 times steeper. blocks.text: If the current pace holds, OpenAI would cover the drop in log-perplexity from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4.1, which took three years, in about six and a half months. This acceleration is even more striking because progress in loss should get harder over time: text is never perfectly predictable, so the loss can’t fall below some floor, and gains typically become smaller as models approach it. Under standard scaling laws, each tenfold increase in compute buys a smaller drop in loss than the last, so naively we would expect progress in loss to slow down over time (see figure below).1

blocks.text: Among METR staff there remains active discussion on how to interpret this dramatic acceleration in pretraining progress, and how to reconcile it with the lack of a comparable acceleration in benchmark scores of OpenAI’s models, e.g. as reflected in Epoch’s ECI.

Epoch’s ECI

blocks.text: Concretely, it remains arguable how much this new information should change our forecasts of future AI capabilities. The following considerations are important:

inlines.text: Concretely, it remains arguable how much this new information should change our forecasts of future AI capabilities. The following considerations are important:
It is possible that the data released overstates true progress in pretraining, e.g. through various types of overfitting. More data would help substantially here.

It is possible that benchmark scores are the best measure of real-world capabilities, and pretraining perplexity is only informative as an input. This implies the new data showing acceleration in pretraining progress would not substantially change our forecasts of future capabilities.
However, to the extent that AI contributed to the acceleration in pretraining, this gives us a sign of AI’s likely future contribution to all parts of the model-training pipeline.

It is possible that pretraining perplexity reflects a fundamentally deeper measure of model capability than the typical benchmarks used to evaluate models. Many AI researchers treat pretraining perplexity in this way, and expect that OpenAI’s rapid acceleration in pretraining will be followed by an acceleration in capabilities measured by real-world impact.

blocks.text: There remain substantial disagreements on how much this information should modify our projections of the future path of capabilities, and METR does not have a consensus view on this. Some interpretations imply that OpenAI’s data on acceleration in pretraining should make us expect a broad-based acceleration in real-world AI capabilities over the next six months.

blocks.text: To our knowledge, no frontier developer had previously published how the pretraining loss of its successive frontier models has changed over multiple years on a fixed held-out dataset. This information is typically considered highly commercially sensitive. However, we think publishing information about pretraining loss is very valuable for informing the public about the prospect of AI R&D acceleration. We encourage all AI developers to do the same, as Microsoft has since done for its own models using OpenAI’s dataset, and to share additional context that would let external researchers better understand the degree of acceleration, what’s driving it, and whether we should expect it to continue and/or compound.5

inlines.text: To our knowledge, no frontier developer had previously published how the pretraining loss of its successive frontier models has changed over multiple years on a fixed held-out dataset. This information is typically considered highly commercially sensitive. However, we think publishing information about pretraining loss is very valuable for informing the public about the prospect of AI R&D acceleration. We encourage all AI developers to do the same, as Microsoft has since
done

for its own models using OpenAI’s dataset, and to share additional context that would let external researchers better understand the degree of acceleration, what’s driving it, and whether we should expect it to continue and/or compound.

blocks.text: The following would be especially informative:

inlines.text: The following would be especially informative:
Log-perplexity on other held-out datasets.

Loss measured on a single corpus may not capture progress on other kinds of text. OpenAI’s plot, for example, reports loss on a corpus sourced from its own internal codebase. Recent recipes or data could help on that kind of text (e.g. coding) more than on others, or small parts of the codebase could have leaked into training data. Log-perplexity on other very different held-out datasets (e.g. a corpus of books) would be informative about the robustness of this trend.
Eventually, these held-out corpora could be maintained by a third party, making it possible to compare trends in pretraining loss across AI developers.
The rough date that the pretraining run ended for each model.

Plotting models at their public release dates may not capture when pretraining progress happened: log-perplexity is a property of the base model, and base models could be finished months before release. If the lag between the end of the pretraining run and model release shrank over time, the acceleration in loss would be smaller than the plot suggests (and vice versa). More importantly, knowing the lag helps us determine how much AI uplift contributed to the pretraining gains: regardless of when a model was released, we can’t attribute its pretraining gains to AI agents if its pretraining happened when researchers barely used AI agents.
How pretraining compute, labor spending, and experiment compute changed over time.

Lower pretraining loss could be attributable to a number of factors: for example, increased training compute, increased labor or experimental compute spending, or increased uplift from AI assistance. Some of these factors imply that we should expect the growth to be a one-time spike, while others imply that we should expect it to continue; if it is substantially attributable to AI uplift, the acceleration could compound. To understand this, it would be helpful to have a sense of how these resources were growing in the relevant time period.
Footnotes

One way to see this is to convert log-perplexity into “effective compute”: the compute that a single fixed recipe would need to reach a given loss value. If we assumed that all of OpenAI’s models are on the same scaling law with irreducible loss between 0.3 and 0.6, effective compute would have grown roughly 8 to 10 times faster since early 2026 than in 2022–2025, measured in orders of magnitude per year. However, that assumption is unrealistic, since newer recipes likely follow different scaling laws.

For example, architectural changes that spend more computation per token, such as looped transformers, might lower perplexity more than they improve downstream capabilities, since standard models could reach similar capabilities after post-training by reasoning in a chain of thought.
A footnote

in OpenAI’s post is consistent with AI playing a small role at the start of the acceleration, but a larger role currently: “We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI.” Similarly, METR’s recent
assessment

of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic found that the acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors, but estimated that “a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI.”
A related argument why this data on pretraining acceleration should modify our forecasts of real-world capabilities is that our scales of capability, such as ECI,
MCI
, and time horizon, are sensitive to delicate statistical assumptions, or rely heavily on a few benchmarks that are close to saturation.
Many other kinds of information would also help, but we have focused on a few numbers that we expect companies already collect and should be relatively simple to share.

The other held-out datasets should date from before 2022, so that they don’t contain any AI-generated text. Ideally, they would cover a variety of text types, such as code, scientific writing, and prose, to show how much of the trend on the original held-out set reflects progress on code specifically.
